findings.source_passage: Sir Leicester has no objection to an interminable Chancery suit. It is a slow, expensive, British, constitutional kind of thing. To be sure, he has not a vital interest in the suit in question, her part in which was the only property my Lady brought him
findings.source_locator: paragraph beginning 'Sir Leicester has no objection'
findings.why_it_matters: The parenthetical 'To be sure, he has not a vital interest in the suit in question, her part in which was the only property my Lady brought him' carries interpretive weight about the marriage's financial character and Dickens's ironic undercutting of Sir Leicester; the draft omits this clause entirely, losing both the irony and a plot-relevant detail.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the clause 'To be sure, he has not a vital interest in the suit in question, her part in which was the only property my Lady brought him' before the sentence about his shadowy impression.

findings.source_passage: There is an air of prescription about him which is always agreeable to Sir Leicester; he receives it as a kind of tribute. He likes Mr. Tulkinghorn's dress; there is a kind of tribute in that too. It is eminently respectable, and likewise, in a general way, retainer-like. It expresses, as it were, the steward of the legal mysteries, the butler of the legal cellar, of the Dedlocks.
findings.source_locator: paragraph beginning 'Sir Leicester Dedlock is with my Lady'
findings.why_it_matters: The rhythmic, itemised repetition of 'tribute'/'tribute' and the formal apposition ('steward of the legal mysteries, the butler of the legal cellar') is rhetorically distinctive; the draft collapses it into a single compressed sentence, losing the satirical cadence.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the doubled 'kind of tribute' structure and the full appositive phrase 'steward of the legal mysteries, the butler of the legal cellar, of the Dedlocks' rather than the abbreviated version.

findings.source_passage: (Sir Leicester was going to Paris too, by the by, but the delight of the fashionable intelligence was in his Lady.)
findings.source_locator: parenthetical after Tulkinghorn mentions 'I see you are going to Paris'
findings.why_it_matters: This parenthetical aside is a characteristic Dickensian satirical interjection mocking fashionable intelligence's gendered obsession; its absence removes a small but voice-defining ironic beat.
findings.suggested_fix: Insert the parenthetical '(Sir Leicester was going to Paris too, by the by, but the delight of the fashionable intelligence was in his Lady.)' after the affidavit speech.

summary: The draft preserves all major signature passages faithfully—the Rip Van Winkle metaphor, the jeweller's-cotton paragraph, the Ghost's Walk drip, the Alexander/freezing-mood passage, the Tulkinghorn mausoleum passage, and the Sladdery/Blaze-and-Sparkle satirical set-piece—with only minor flattening of the Sir Leicester/Tulkinghorn tribute paragraph, omission of the Paris parenthetical, and loss of one ironic Chancery clause; no high-severity failures found.
